title: How the Bible was gathered
hookLine: letters passed hand to hand and read aloud, until the churches knew which books were theirs

cards: At the end of a letter to a small church in Colossae, Paul adds a note about the mail. When this letter has been read to you, he says, send it on to the church at Laodicea, and read the one from Laodicea too.
A scroll, read aloud to a room of people, then rolled up and carried down the road to the next room. That's the Bible before it was a book. Day one hundred twenty-five called it a library.
Today: how the Bible was gathered.

teach.b: The Bible didn't arrive as a bound volume.
Luke's Gospel opens by admitting there were other accounts: "Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us." Many.
Luke wasn't the only one writing, and the churches had to come to know which writings were theirs. Christians often describe it the way Paul's note suggests: by reading.

The writings churches kept reading aloud, Sunday after Sunday, that they trusted as coming from the apostles and their circle, and that matched the faith they'd been taught, came to be called scripture.
You can watch it start inside the Bible. The second letter of Peter mentions Paul's letters, which some people twist, "as they do also the other scriptures." Paul's mail, set beside the scriptures.
Over time, bishops and councils wrote the books down in lists. One that survives is a letter Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, sent his churches at Easter.
He names the books of both testaments, calls them fountains of salvation, and adds that no one should add to them or take from them.

Churches still differ on some books. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include books such as Tobit and the Maccabees in the Old Testament; Protestant Bibles leave them out or print them apart, as the Apocrypha.
Catholics and Orthodox stress the church recognizing the books; Protestants stress the books carrying their own authority, which the church came to see. Both say the church didn't invent the Bible.

how: Christians receive the Bible as the books the church read and recognized in worship; Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include some Old Testament books that Protestant Bibles leave out or print separately as the Apocrypha.

games.q: you're in an early church, and a letter from an apostle has just been read aloud to your congregation. what happens to it next?
o: it's locked away so no one else sees it.
it's sent on down the road to be read in another church.
it's burned, since everyone has heard it now.
games.why: Paul tells the Colossians to send their letter on to Laodicea and read the one coming from there. sharing and reading aloud is how the books traveled.

practice: Open a Bible, or a Bible app, to the contents page: a list, like the one Athanasius sent his churches.

Read the names slowly, one at a time, Genesis, Ruth, Psalms, Mark, Romans, each one read aloud in rooms full of people long before it was printed there. If you pray, give thanks for the readers; if not, just let the names go by.

wordCard.voice: How the Bible was gathered: not voted into being in one afternoon, but read aloud in worship until the churches knew which books were theirs, and then written down in lists.

carryVoice: Your line: the church read these. Heard first, then written down in lists. Back tomorrow, same hill.
